study.title: Light and Hiding
study.focus: Why do people run from the light, and what does it look like to come to it?
study.take: This take follows the heart: condemnation is not Christ's aim, yet people choose the dark (3:18-20), and the one who does truth walks toward the light (3:21).
study.closing: What is one thing you tend to keep in the dark, and what would it mean to bring it to the light?

scripture.18: He who believes in him is not judged. He who doesn’t believe has been judged already, because he has not believed in the name of the only born Son of God.
scripture.19: This is the judgment, that the light has come into the world, and men loved the darkness rather than the light, for their works were evil.
scripture.20: For everyone who does evil hates the light and doesn’t come to the light, lest his works would be exposed.
scripture.21: But he who does the truth comes to the light, that his works may be revealed, that they have been done in God.”

verse_questions.18: Condemned already: what does that mean?
verse_questions.20: What does the light expose, and why does that feel threatening?
verse_questions.21: What does coming to the light look like?

summaries.CAL3.18.03: John Calvin says the words condemned already stress that unbelievers are utterly ruined. He adds that Christ speaks especially of people whose wickedness shows itself in open contempt for the gospel.
summaries.JFB3.18.01: Jamieson, Fausset and Brown say the believer has passed from death to life the moment he believes. The one who is condemned already is the one who rejects the single way out that God gave his Son to provide, and so chooses to stay condemned.
summaries.MHC3.18.03: Matthew Henry reads here the fate of those who will not believe in Christ: they are already condemned. Their sin is serious because of the one they dismiss, the only Son of God, who is completely true and good and deserves to be believed and embraced. God sent the one dearest to himself to save us, so shouldn't he be dearest to us?
summaries.CAL3.19.02: John Calvin says people think it harsh that those who do not believe in Christ are doomed. So that no one blames Christ for his own condemnation, John shows that each person should blame himself, since unbelief is a sign of a bad conscience. It is their own wickedness that keeps unbelievers from coming to Christ.
summaries.MHC3.19.04: Matthew Henry says humanity's fall began in a desire for forbidden knowledge and is kept alive by a desire for forbidden ignorance. People love their sickness and their slavery and will not be made free or whole. The true reason they love darkness is that their deeds are evil: they think darkness excuses their deeds, and they hate the light because it takes away the good opinion they had of themselves by showing them their sin and misery.
summaries.JFB3.19.01: Jamieson, Fausset and Brown say this is the condemnation in a strong sense: it reveals a condemnation that already exists and seals in it those who will not be delivered from it. The light has come into the world in the person of Jesus himself. They add that loving darkness can only be known by deliberately rejecting Christ, but that rejection reveals it in a frightening way.
summaries.CHR3.19.2.01: Chrysostom points out that Jesus takes away every excuse when he says the light came into the world. Did they seek it themselves, he asks, or work to find it? The light itself came to them, and even so they would not hurry toward it.
summaries.MHC3.20.06: Matthew Henry puts it simply: Christ is hated because sin is loved. People who do not come to the light show a secret hatred of it; if they did not resist saving knowledge, they would not sit so contentedly in ruinous ignorance.
summaries.CAL3.20.01: John Calvin explains that the light is hateful to such people only because they are wicked and want to hide their sins. By rejecting the remedy, they deliberately feed the very ground of their condemnation. He warns that we are mistaken if we think those who rage against the gospel are moved by godly zeal; they actually avoid the light so that they can flatter themselves more freely in the dark.
summaries.GIL3.20.02: John Gill says the person who does evil avoids the light for fear his deeds will be exposed, that he will be shamed and blamed, and that he will be told to give them up, which he does not want to do.
summaries.JFB3.20.01: Jamieson, Fausset and Brown define reproved here as exposed by detection.
summaries.JFB3.21.01: Jamieson, Fausset and Brown describe the one who does truth as someone whose only aim in life is to be and do what can stand the light. He loves the light and comes to it so that everything about him, thoroughly tested, may be seen to be divinely wrought and divinely approved.
summaries.MHC3.21.02: Matthew Henry describes the character of a good man: he does truth, acting sincerely in all he does. He may sometimes fall short of the good he wants to do, and he has his weaknesses, but he aims honestly and holds on to his integrity. And he is one who comes to the light.
summaries.CAL3.21.03: John Calvin says Christ uses the word truth because we are easily fooled by the outward shine of good works and do not look at what is hidden inside. Upright people, free from hypocrisy, willingly come into the presence of God, who alone is the fit judge of our works. Works are called done in God when he approves them and they are good by his standard.
summaries.AUG3.19-21.2.05: Augustine says we begin to do the truth when we stop soothing and flattering ourselves and stop calling ourselves righteous while we are not. Coming to the light means letting our works be shown for what they are. Even the displeasure we feel at our own sin is God's doing: it would not trouble us unless God shone into us and his truth showed it to us.

labels.jewish_source: A later Jewish writing that Gill cites; not a statement of what people believed in Jesus's day.
